lesson.title: The Newspaper Campaign That Explained a Constitution
lesson.summary: The Federalist Papers, eighty-five essays published under the name Publius in 1787 and 1788, laid out the reasoning behind the Constitution's federalist structure to persuade skeptical New York voters to support ratification.
lesson.body:
Once the Constitutional Convention finished its work in September 1787, the document still needed to be ratified by conventions in at least nine of the thirteen states before it could take effect, and nothing about that outcome was guaranteed. New York was one of the states where the outcome felt genuinely uncertain, with a governor, George Clinton, who leaned toward the Anti-Federalist camp and a public still digesting arguments on both sides.

Alexander Hamilton, who had represented New York at the convention despite frequently losing votes to his own state's other delegates, decided the Constitution needed a sustained, systematic defense written for ordinary newspaper readers rather than fellow delegates. He recruited James Madison, whose deep involvement in shaping the Constitution's federalist structure made him uniquely qualified to explain it, and John Jay, an experienced diplomat, though illness limited Jay to contributing only a handful of essays. Publishing under the shared pen name Publius, a reference to a founder of the Roman Republic, the three men produced eighty-five essays between October 1787 and August 1788, appearing first in New York newspapers before being collected into a book.

Hamilton wrote the largest share, roughly fifty-one essays, with Madison contributing around twenty-nine and Jay the remaining few. The essays walked through the new Constitution clause by clause, defending its structure against Anti-Federalist objections and explaining the reasoning behind choices like the division of powers between the states and the national government. Several individual essays became especially influential over time. Federalist No. 10, written by Madison, argued that a large republic spanning many states and interests was actually better protected against the dangers of factions than a small one, since no single faction could easily dominate such a broad and diverse country.

Federalist No. 51, also Madison's, laid out the logic of checks and balances, explaining how dividing power among branches of government that could each check the others would help prevent any one branch from becoming too powerful, famously describing the goal as making ambition counteract ambition. Federalist No. 78, written by Hamilton, defended the judiciary and described the courts as the weakest of the three branches since they controlled neither the sword nor the purse, while also laying groundwork for the idea that courts could strike down laws that conflicted with the Constitution.

New York's ratifying convention approved the Constitution in July 1788, and while historians debate exactly how much credit the essays themselves deserve for that outcome, the Federalist Papers have far outlasted their original purpose. They remain one of the most cited sources for understanding what the framers intended the Constitution's federalist structure to accomplish, studied today by judges, scholars, and students well beyond the New York readers they were originally written to convince.
